description: Line maintenance of commercial aircraft: deferrals, release to service, inspections, tooling, parts and duty limits.

units.title: Minimum equipment list (MEL)
units.text: An approved list of equipment that may be inoperative at departure, together with the conditions and time limits under which the aircraft can still fly. Anything not on the list must be repaired before the next flight.

units.title: MEL repair categories
units.text:
| Category | Repair interval |
|---|---|
| A | As stated in the item remarks |
| B | 3 consecutive calendar days |
| C | 10 consecutive calendar days |
| D | 120 consecutive calendar days |

units.title: Certificate of release to service
units.text: After any maintenance task, a licensed engineer signs a certificate of release to service before the aircraft may fly. A mechanic without a licence may do the work but cannot sign the release.

units.title: Independent inspection of flight controls
units.text: Any disturbance of a flight control system requires an independent inspection by a second qualified person who did not perform the task. The aircraft cannot be released until both signatures are on the task card.

units.title: Tool control prevents foreign object damage
headingPath: Tool control prevents foreign object damage
units.text: Every tool sits on a shadow board and is counted at the end of a task. A missing tool stops the release of the aircraft until it is found, because a tool left in an engine or a control run can cause serious damage.

units.title: A-check
units.text: A light scheduled inspection carried out roughly every 600 flight hours, usually overnight at a line station. It covers a general visual inspection, fluids, filters and the deferred MEL items.

units.title: Bird strike inspection
units.text: After a reported bird strike, engineers inspect the impact area, the engine inlet and the fan blades. If the bird hit an engine, a borescope inspection of that engine is done before the next flight.

units.title: Tyre limits
units.text: A tyre is replaced when the tread is worn to the bottom of any groove or when a cut exposes the cord. Tyre pressure is checked with the tyres cold before the first flight of each day.

units.title: Engineer duty limits
units.text: Maintenance engineers may work at most 12 hours in a duty period and must have at least 11 hours of rest between duties.

units.title: Fleet reliability
units.text:
| Indicator | Target | 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| Technical dispatch reliability | 99.5% | 99.2% |
| Deferred defects per aircraft | Below 4 | 5.1 |
| Repeat defects | Below 2% | 2.6% |

units.title: Repeat defects
units.text: A defect that occurs three times on the same aircraft within 15 flight cycles is classified as a repeat defect and escalated to the reliability engineer for a root-cause investigation.

units.title: Unapproved parts are never installed
units.text: Every installed part must come with an authorised release certificate that traces it to an approved manufacturer or repair station. A part without that certificate is quarantined, even if it looks new.

units.title: Hangar movements in high wind
units.text: When gusts exceed 40 knots, towing aircraft into or out of the hangar is suspended and the hangar doors stay closed.

units.title: Engine ground runs
units.text: Only engineers who hold an engine-run authorisation may run engines on the ground, and any run above idle power takes place at the designated run-up area.
